title: Joining Woody Herman and switching to baritone
summary: Glen Drews recommended him and Bill Byrne called; he bought a baritone and joined in Bridgeport in May 1978, sitting next to Joe Lovano, and describes Herman's forward-looking approach.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Let me ask you about, I think what was a sort of important milestone in your career with Woody Herman. Do you recall the phone call? Who called you about being on that band?

It was Bill Byrne who was the trumpet. He was the band manager. And he called — well let me preface the story, I was playing on Long Island with, well it was called the Long Island Jazz Quintet at this time. This was 1978. And it was Glen Drews who was playing trumpet, actually he’s the one that got called to play with Woody first. So Glen Drews the trumpet player, he left our group and he was on Woody’s band. And a couple of months later the phone rang and it was Bill Byrne, who was the road manager and the fifth trumpet player. Glen Drews had recommended me to join the band. So that’s how they kind of found out about me first. And they asked me if I wanted to join first of all, and I mean that was kind of why I was playing in the first place, trying to get a gig like that, to go out and play. So they were on the road 50 weeks a year. They played all the time, and all kinds of really amazingly interesting places. One day he played an Elks Club for a dance, and the next night he’d be at Carnegie Hall. The next day he’d play like at a VFW, the next night he’d play in a high school auditorium in a gym, and the next night he’d play in a symphony hall in Chicago, the next night he’d play at a jazz festival, the next night he’d play — you know it was like really an eye opening experience in terms of what it’s like to be a musician. Because you have to be a jack of all trades. You have to play for all kinds of people in all kinds of different places, and still play at that level. Woody Herman was like, wow, I can’t even begin to speak about what an influence he was, just in terms of how you have to be well rounded and how you have to act and behave as a musician on the bandstand. It was a really amazing lesson. So as I say I got the call and I’d never played baritone. This is when I switched to baritone. So I went out and bought a baritone, a Yamaha baritone with a low A and two weeks later after I got the call, it was May 25, 1978, I joined the band in Bridgeport, Connecticut. I took my horn out of the case and I was so nervous. Because first of all Woody’s — one of his biggest pet peeves was alto saxophone players who play baritone. I found this out later. He hated that. And that was describing me to a tee. And you know this was the first time I was ever going to play the baritone in public. So I took the baritone out of the case and sat down next to Joe Lovano. He was in the chair next to me. And so but that was it. It © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

was like “Four Brothers” boom. Early on, here we go. And it was a great band. Mark Johnson was playing bass and he was, at that time, auditioning for the job of Bill Evans, which he got. John Riley was playing drums who now is playing in the Vanguard Jazz Orchestra sitting in Mel Lewis’ seat, Frank Tiberi of course, Dave LaLama, Ralph’s brother on piano. It was really an incredible band. And the other thing that struck me about Woody that was really inspiring was how forward thinking he was. He didn’t live in the past at all. I mean he was into all kinds of modern music. He had commissioned Chic Corea to write a three movement suite for the band that we actually played a lot, and he loved the music of Steeley Dan, we did a Steeley Dan record called “Aja.” So he was not somebody who was just content to just play his big hits from the past. He really had one foot in the past and certainly one foot in the future. So he was — and what a talent scout. I mean look at all the people who went through that band, from the forties all the way up until he passed. I mean it’s a veritable who’s who of music. So just being able to be on the bandstand with him really was an honor and a privilege, and I still feel blessed to have had that opportunity because it’s also — that’s when I became a baritone player, those two years, then I really loved the baritone. And he didn’t fire me. So he must have seen some germ of something there, some potential. I didn’t play the alto anymore after that.
